text: Every pattern in this chapter eventually gets written down as a runbook — which alarms fire, who gets paged, which commands promote the secondary, what order services come back up in. Writing that runbook feels like finishing the job. It isn't, because a document describes what should happen, and says nothing about whether it actually happens. Only running it proves that.

Infrastructure drifts constantly, and a document doesn't drift with it. The DR region's state can fall behind production's. A hardcoded IP written eighteen months ago can point at something that no longer exists. A credential scoped to the DR environment can expire quietly. The engineer who wrote the runbook can leave, taking undocumented context with them. None of that shows up by rereading the document — only by running it.

A tabletop exercise — walking through the runbook as a group, narrating each step without executing it — is cheap and worth doing regularly. It surfaces a missing owner, an ambiguous escalation path, a step nobody present can explain. But it can't catch what only shows up in execution: a DNS record with a longer TTL than remembered, a connection string still hardcoded to the primary region, an IAM role in the DR account missing a permission the runbook assumes it has.

A real drill means actually failing something over — production itself on a planned schedule, or at minimum a production-like environment exercising the same infrastructure and the same runbook steps. That's the practice behind game days and chaos engineering: deliberately triggering the failure you're defending against, on your own schedule, so you control the blast radius. It's also the only way to actually measure RTO and RPO rather than estimate them — you start a clock and watch what the real numbers turn out to be.

The instinct to avoid running a real test, because a failure looks bad, is exactly backwards. A test that fails found a real gap — an expired credential, a missing permission — before a real disaster found it instead, with no controlled way to recover. An untested plan carries that same risk invisibly; the only difference is nobody has discovered it yet.

Treating scheduled failover drills as routine, repeated as the environment keeps changing, is what keeps a DR plan describing a system that still actually works. With resilience now something you design for and actually prove, Chapter 4 is complete — next, Governance at Scale turns to policy as code, tagging, and the guardrails that keep an entire organization's cloud footprint under control.
